The proposed direction is to prove that for a finite closure system equipped with a potential compatible with closure enlargement, any reconstruction procedure driven by closure-stable probes yields a descending potential sequence, hence terminates within a bound determined by the initial potential. Concretely, define a reconstruction state space of partial information, a one-step probe update operator, and prove three linked results: correctness (the limit state recovers the target closed set), monotonicity (each nontrivial update strictly decreases a natural defect potential, or dually increases recovered information), and complexity (the number of updates is bounded by the initial potential, giving an `InfoEfficientAlgorithm`). It can fail if the proposed potential is not strictly compatible with probe refinement, so the theorem must identify exact hypotheses under which the bound is valid.

concept.title: The Prime Number Crossword: Filling the Gaps in the Primes
concept.concept_description: Prime gaps — the spaces between consecutive primes — are like empty cells in a crossword puzzle. The gaps are 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, ... (OEIS A001223). The pattern seems random, but the crossword has rules: (1) All prime gaps are even (except the first gap of 1 between 2 and 3). (2) A gap g can only appear at position n if n+g is prime and all of n+1, n+2, ..., n+g-1 are composite. (3) The density of gap g near n is approximately 2*C_2/(g*log(n)) where C_2 is the twin prime constant. Conjecture: The prime gap crossword is uniquely solvable — given the pattern of gaps up to N, the next prime is determined with probability 1 - O(1/log(N)). More precisely, the conditional probability that the next prime after p is p + g, given all primes up to p, is approximately 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p)) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2). This is the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for prime gaps. But the crossword has a surprise: certain gap patterns FORCE the next number. For example, if the gaps near n are 6, 4, 2, 6, then the next gap is almost certainly 4 (the only way to fill the crossword).
